claim_verdicts.evidence: `git -C examples/don-hang show stage-1:DonHang.Infrastructure/DonHangDbContext.cs` lines 9-14: Customers, Products, Orders, OrderItems, Payments, Notifications, each expression-bodied over `Set<T>()`. Line 10 is exactly `public DbSet<Product> Products => Set<Product>();`, the string §5 quotes inline. Live `psql \dt` on donhang-db lists exactly those six application tables (plus EF's own `__EFMigrationsHistory`, which has no DbSet and is the migrations lesson's subject). Tag stage-1 -> commit 4fca60a.

refs/efcore-docs/entity-framework/core/index.md line 22: "With EF Core, data access is performed using a model. A model is made up of entity classes and a context object that represents a session with the database. The context object allows querying and saving data." Line 34: "Instances of your entity classes are retrieved from the database using Language Integrated Query (LINQ)." Supports §3's `DbContext` bullet ("asking it for data returns C# objects, not the rows a query hands back").

Verbatim, refs/efcore-docs/entity-framework/core/modeling/entity-properties.md line 30 ("Column names"): "By convention, when using a relational database, entity properties are mapped to table columns having the same name as the property." Followed by "If you prefer to configure your columns with different names..." with Data Annotations and Fluent API tabs. The negative form in section 4 also holds: core/extensions/index.md line 154 lists snake_case naming as a third-party plugin, and grep of what-is-new/ef-core-10.0/ for "naming convention"/"snake" returns nothing.

`git show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/Entities.cs` lines 17-22 are character-for-character the lesson's first code block (`public sealed class Product` + `Id`, `required string Name`, `PriceVnd`). Exactly three properties, no attributes, no base class; the file opens with `namespace DonHang.Domain;` and has no using of Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore — nothing in the class refers to a database. §5's "Three properties, no attributes, no base class" is true of this code.

DonHangDbContext.cs lines 30-36 match the lesson's second block character-for-character, 8-space indentation included: `modelBuilder.Entity<Product>(e => { e.ToTable("products"); e.Property(p => p.Id).HasColumnName("id"); e.Property(p => p.Name).HasColumnName("name"); e.Property(p => p.PriceVnd).HasColumnName("price_vnd"); });`. Documented shape: refs/efcore-docs samples/core/Modeling/EntityProperties/FluentAPI/ColumnName.cs, and modeling/entity-types.md line 50 for the table-name convention `ToTable` overrides.

issues.text: "Case counts as a difference" is true here because of PostgreSQL, not because of anything EF Core checks. EF Core never compares names against the database: it puts the configured (or default) name into the SQL, Npgsql quotes identifiers, and PostgreSQL treats `"Id"` and `id` as different columns. Verified live: `select "Id" from products` -> `ERROR:  column "Id" does not exist`. On a case-insensitive database the same three properties would map without `HasColumnName`, so the rule as stated is broader than the pinned stack supports.
issues.quote: Case counts as a difference, the same way `PriceVnd` and `price_vnd` do
issues.fix: Tie it to this database: "Against this PostgreSQL database, case counts as a difference, the same way `PriceVnd` and `price_vnd` do…". Optionally extend claim 7 with the second live check (`select "Id" from products` -> `column "Id" does not exist`).

issues.text: The key (c) is the right answer, but its reason names a step that does not exist: nothing compares the two names. EF Core uses the property's own spelling as the column name (modeling/entity-properties.md line 30: "entity properties are mapped to table columns having the same name as the property") and PostgreSQL is what reports the missing column. A reader who takes "compared as plain strings" literally will look for a comparison EF Core never performs. Options a, b and d remain correctly wrong.
issues.quote: False, because the two names are compared as plain strings, so the mapping has to name `price_vnd` itself.
issues.fix: Reword option c (en and vi): "False — EF Core uses the property's own spelling as the column name, so the mapping has to name `price_vnd` itself." Key stays `c`.

issues.text: The key (a) is right, but its second branch does not happen on this stack. There is no path where the query succeeds and the property is merely left without a real value; that outcome is what option c (wrongly) describes.
